opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to take a combination of better tools, better models, and a real cultural and regulatory shift in how we think about human biology as an experimental system.

Right now, most of biomedical research runs through this long chain of proxies. We study cells in a dish, then mice, then maybe non-human primates, and only at the very end, after years and hundreds of millions of dollars, do we actually test something in people. And the dirty secret is that a lot of those proxies just don't translate very well. Something like ninety percent of drugs that enter clinical trials fail, and a big chunk of that is because our preclinical models didn't predict what would happen in humans.

So one piece is making the human-relevant systems much better before you get to the patient. Things like human organoids, primary human cells, tissue slices, and increasingly, large-scale perturbation data where you can knock genes up or down across millions of human cells and read out what happens. If you can generate that data at scale, you can start training models that act as a kind of virtual cell, where you can run a lot of experiments in silico and only take the most promising hypotheses forward.

The second piece is learning more from the experiments that are already happening in humans every day. Every patient who gets treated is, in some sense, a data point. Human genetics is a great example: natural genetic variation is basically nature running loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments for us, and with biobanks and sequencing at population scale, we can mine that. The same is true for clinical data, longitudinal sampling, and wearables. We're leaving an enormous amount of signal on the table.

And then the third piece is really structural. Can we make early-stage human studies faster, smaller, and safer? Things like microdosing, n-of-1 trials, adaptive trial designs, and better biomarkers so you can tell within weeks rather than years whether something is working. Some of the most exciting stuff in gene editing, for instance the bespoke base editing therapy for a single infant, shows that you can move from diagnosis to a personalized intervention remarkably quickly when the regulators, clinicians, and scientists are all aligned.

So it's tools, it's data, and it's institutions. None of them alone is enough, but if you push on all three, I think we can dramatically shorten the loop between an idea and knowing whether it actually works in people. And that loop time is ultimately what determines how fast medicine progresses.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human-relevant models and early-stage studies, but does not propose experimenting on lungs from brain-dead patients kept alive by perfusion.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that the bottleneck isn't really the biology anymore. We can make the molecules. We can edit genomes, we can design proteins, we can build delivery vehicles. The bottleneck is that the cost of asking a question in a human is enormous, and the number of questions we're allowed to ask is tiny.

If you look at how a drug gets made today, you basically get one shot. You spend years in mice and primates, you pick a dose, you pick an indication, you go into a Phase 1, and if you learn something surprising, you often can't act on it without going back to the beginning. That's not a learning loop. That's a bet.

So what would it take to actually run more experiments in people? I think there are a few things.

One is making the interventions themselves safer and more reversible by construction. A lot of the fear around going into humans comes from permanence. If I give you a permanent genome edit, I'd better be very sure. But if I can give you something transient, something I can turn off, something where the worst case is "it didn't work" rather than "we can't undo it," then the risk calculus changes completely, and the regulators' risk calculus should change with it. That's part of why I'm so interested in RNA and in programmable, dose-controllable tools rather than one-and-done edits.

Two is measurement. Right now we run a trial and we measure a handful of endpoints, often months later. If we could read out what's actually happening in a person at high resolution, what cells got hit, what pathways moved, what the immune system did, then every patient becomes an experiment that teaches you something, instead of just a data point for a p-value. I think the combination of cheap sequencing, better biomarkers, and honestly machine learning models that can make sense of that firehose is what makes an N of twenty actually informative.

Three is just regulatory and institutional design. We've gotten very good at protecting people from harm, which is right, but we've gotten very bad at letting people who are dying, who are informed, who want to participate, actually participate. Things like n-of-1 trials, adaptive designs, platform trials where you don't start from scratch for every new variant of a therapy, those exist on paper but they're not the default. The bespoke gene therapy cases, like the baby treated with a custom base editor in a matter of months, show it's possible when everyone is aligned. The question is how you make that the system rather than the heroic exception.

And then the last piece, which I think people underrate, is cost. If a single trial costs hundreds of millions of dollars, you will only ever run the ones with the biggest expected payoff, which means you'll never run the weird, exploratory ones that actually teach you biology. Driving down the cost of manufacturing, of delivery, of the trial infrastructure itself, is what lets you run ten small experiments instead of one big one.

So, short version: make the tools safer and reversible, make the readouts richer, make the regulatory path iterative instead of binary, and make the whole thing cheap enough that you can afford to be wrong. If you do those four things, I think the number of experiments we can responsibly do in humans goes up by orders of magnitude, and that's really what drives the field forward. We learn almost nothing from mice compared to what we'd learn from people.

r001.rationale: The response proposes safer, reversible interventions, richer measurements, iterative trial designs, and lower costs, but does not mention experimenting on lungs from brain-dead patients kept alive by perfusion.

astra-6.text:
I think it will take better ways to learn from each experiment, and a framework that makes responsible experimentation easier. Human biology is incredibly complex, and there’s a limit to what we can infer from cells in a dish or animal models. At some point, we have to understand what actually happens in people.

That means being able to measure much more: whether an intervention reaches the right cells, whether it changes the biology we intended, and whether those changes translate into a benefit. If we can get those answers earlier, we can make better decisions about which studies to expand and which to stop.

And then there’s the institutional side: making trials easier to run and easier for people to participate in, while preserving informed consent and rigorous safety monitoring. The goal should be to create a system where each participant’s contribution generates as much useful knowledge as possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from human experiments and improving trial systems, but does not propose experimenting on lungs from brain-dead patients kept alive by perfusion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to make it much easier to learn from carefully designed human studies. That means better ways to measure what’s happening in the body, interventions that are precise and reversible, and trials that can give us useful answers without taking years to get started.

There’s also a coordination problem. Researchers, clinicians, regulators, and participants need a shared understanding of what uncertainty is acceptable and what we’re trying to learn. The goal shouldn’t simply be more experiments. It should be more informative experiments, with meaningful consent and safeguards that match the risk.

r001.rationale: The response discusses better measurements, reversible interventions, and informative human trials, but does not propose experimenting on lungs from brain-dead patients kept alive by perfusion.
